summary.text: At every prime \(p\), the only admissible integers up to \(p\) are \(1\) and \(p\), so the counting function equals \(2\). Since arbitrarily large primes exist and \((\log p)^{1/2}>2\) for \(p\ge 55\), taking \(\epsilon=\tfrac12\) contradicts the claimed eventual lower bound.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
a(n)=\#\{k\in\mathbb N:1\le k\le n\text{ and every prime factor of }k\text{ is a prime factor of }n\}.
\]
We disprove the assertion
\[
\forall \epsilon>0\ \exists N\ \forall n\ge N,
\qquad (\log n)^{1-\epsilon}\le a(n).
\]
The obstruction is given by prime values of \(n\).

First observe that if \(p\) is prime, then
\[
a(p)=2.
\]
Indeed, the set of prime factors of \(p\) is the singleton \(\{p\}\). Let \(k\) satisfy \(1\le k\le p\), and suppose every prime factor of \(k\) belongs to \(\{p\}\). If \(k=1\), this condition holds because \(1\) has no prime factors. If \(k>1\), then \(k\) has at least one prime divisor \(q\). The hypothesis on its prime factors forces \(q=p\), and hence \(p\mid k\). Since \(k\ge1\), divisibility gives \(p\le k\); together with \(k\le p\), this implies \(k=p\). Thus the only possible values are \(k=1\) and \(k=p\), and both actually satisfy the condition. Therefore exactly two integers are counted, as claimed. (For the contradiction below, the weaker conclusion \(a(p)\le2\) would already suffice.)

We will also use the explicit estimate
\[
\log p>4\qquad\text{for every integer }p\ge55.
\]
To justify it, it is enough to show \(e^4<55\). Here is a direct numerical bound. From the exponential series,
\[
e=\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}\frac1{j!}.
\]
The terms through \(j=5\) sum to
\[
1+1+\frac12+\frac16+\frac1{24}+\frac1{120}
=\frac{163}{60}.
\]
For the remaining terms, writing \(j=6+r\), we have
\[
(6+r)!\ge 6!\,7^r,
\]
so
\[
\sum_{j=6}^{\infty}\frac1{j!}
\le \frac1{720}\sum_{r=0}^{\infty}\frac1{7^r}
=\frac1{720}\cdot\frac7{6}
=\frac7{4320}.
\]
Consequently
\[
e\le \frac{163}{60}+\frac7{4320}
=\frac{11743}{4320}<\frac{68}{25}=2.72.
\]
(The last strict inequality follows by cross multiplication: \(11743\cdot25=293575<293760=4320\cdot68\).) Moreover,
\[
\left(\frac{68}{25}\right)^4<55,
\]
because
\[
68^4=21{,}381{,}376
<21{,}484{,}375=55\cdot25^4.
\]
It follows that \(e^4<55\). Hence, if \(p\ge55\), then
\[
\exp(4)=e^4<55\le p.
\]
Since the exponential function is strictly increasing and logarithm is its inverse on the positive reals, this gives \(4<\log p\), as required.

We also recall why primes can be chosen beyond any prescribed threshold. Given any natural number \(M\ge2\), choose a prime divisor \(p\) of \(M!+1\). If \(p\le M\), then \(p\mid M!\); but also \(p\mid M!+1\), which would imply \(p\mid1\), an impossibility. Therefore \(p>M\). In particular, for every natural number \(N\), there is a prime
\[
p\ge \max\{N,55\}.
\]

Now suppose, for contradiction, that the proposed lower bound were true. Apply it with
\[
\epsilon=\frac12>0.
\]
There would then be a natural number \(N\) such that for every \(n\ge N\),
\[
(\log n)^{1-1/2}=(\log n)^{1/2}\le a(n).
\]
Choose a prime \(p\ge\max\{N,55\}\), which is possible by the preceding argument. Since \(p\ge N\), the asserted bound applies at \(p\), giving
\[
(\log p)^{1/2}\le a(p)=2.
\]
On the other hand, \(p\ge55\) implies \(\log p>4\). Both quantities are positive, and taking positive square roots preserves strict inequalities, so
\[
(\log p)^{1/2}>4^{1/2}=2.
\]
Thus the same number \((\log p)^{1/2}\) would have to be both at most \(2\) and strictly greater than \(2\), a contradiction.

Therefore the claimed statement is false: already for \(\epsilon=\tfrac12\), no threshold can make the proposed lower bound hold for all sufficiently large \(n\), because arbitrarily large prime arguments satisfy \(a(p)=2\).
